questions.q: What is the mathematical formula used to calculate distance if you know the speed of an object and the time it has traveled, along with its SI unit?
questions.a: Distance = Speed $\times$ Time, with the SI unit being meters (m). A student who answers "Distance = Speed / Time" is confusing the distance formula with the speed formula, demonstrating a failure to understand how algebraic rearrangement works when isolating variables.

questions.q: Why must we convert time given in minutes or hours into seconds (or speed into m/s) before performing a distance calculation when using standard SI units?
questions.a: We must convert units so that the time units in the speed denominator cancel out with the time units multiplied during the calculation, leaving only the desired unit of length. A student who says "units do not matter as long as the numbers are correct" fails to understand dimensional analysis and will end up with nonsensical composite units like meter-hours per second.

questions.q: A school bus in Bengaluru travels at a uniform speed of $40\text{ m/s}$ for a duration of $15\text{ seconds}$. Calculate the total distance covered by the bus.
questions.a:
Step 1: Identify given quantities: Speed ($v$) = $40\text{ m/s}$, Time ($t$) = $15\text{ s}$.
Step 2: Identify formula: $Distance = Speed \times Time$.
Step 3: Substitute values: $Distance = 40\text{ m/s} \times 15\text{ s}$.
Step 4: Compute and cancel units: $40 \times 15 = 600$, and the seconds units cancel out ($\text{m/s} \times \text{s} = \text{m}$).
Step 5: Final Answer = $600\text{ m}$. A student who computes $40 / 15$ has used the wrong formula, while one who multiplies $40 \times 15$ and forgets the meter unit has missed dimensional tracking.

questions.q: Two cyclists start at the same point. Cyclist A travels at $10\text{ m/s}$ and Cyclist B travels at $5\text{ m/s}$. If both travel for a distance of $300\text{ meters}$, analyze who will take less time and calculate the exact difference in their arrival times.
questions.a: Cyclist A takes less time because higher speed results in a shorter duration for a fixed distance ($Time = Distance / Speed$). Cyclist A's time is $300\text{ m} / 10\text{ m/s} = 30\text{ s}$, while Cyclist B's time is $300\text{ m} / 5\text{ m/s} = 60\text{ s}$. The difference is $60\text{ s} - 30\text{ s} = 30\text{ seconds}$. A student who states that Cyclist B takes less time has inverted the inverse proportionality between speed and time.

questions.q: A student calculates that a bullock cart moving at $2\text{ m/s}$ covers a distance of $10\text{ meters}$ in $20\text{ seconds}$. Evaluate whether this calculation is physically reasonable and identify any mathematical errors.
questions.a: The calculation is incorrect because $2\text{ m/s} \times 20\text{ s}$ equals $40\text{ meters}$, not $10\text{ meters}$. Alternatively, finding time as $10\text{ m} / 2\text{ m/s}$ yields $5\text{ seconds}$, not $20\text{ seconds}$. A student who accepts $20\text{ seconds}$ as correct fails to check their work using the reverse relationship ($Speed = Distance / Time$: $10/20 = 0.5\text{ m/s} \neq 2\text{ m/s}$).

questions.q: Design a simple indoor classroom experiment using a rolling toy car on a straight floor tile track to determine the time taken to cover a measured distance of $2\text{ meters}$, given that the car moves at a constant speed of $0.5\text{ m/s}$.
questions.a: Mark a starting line and a finishing line exactly $2\text{ meters}$ apart using a measuring tape. Release the toy car from rest (ensuring it reaches a uniform speed of $0.5\text{ m/s}$) and start a stopwatch when it crosses the start line, stopping it at the finish line. Calculate expected time as $Time = Distance / Speed = 2\text{ m} / 0.5\text{ m/s} = 4\text{ seconds}$, then compare your stopwatch reading to test experimental accuracy. A poor answer fails to connect the mathematical formula to physical measurement steps or ignores unit consistency.
